00½Module 0 — the CRE-I lines he re-taught

Lectures 2–4 (27–31 July). Short, but he opened the course with it, so a 1–2 mark conceptual question is fair game. notes

Rate — and the three bases you must not mix up

-r_v=\frac{1}{V}\frac{dN}{dt}\ \left[\frac{\mathrm{mol}}{\mathrm{m^3_{reactor}\,s}}\right],\quad -r_w=\frac{1}{W}\frac{dN}{dt}\ \left[\frac{\mathrm{mol}}{\mathrm{kg_{cat}\,s}}\right],\quad -r_s=\frac{1}{S}\frac{dN}{dt}\ \left[\frac{\mathrm{mol}}{\mathrm{m^2_{cat}\,s}}\right] \boxed{(-r_v)V=(-r_w)W=(-r_s)S}

Same physical event, three book-keeping bases. In heterogeneous work the mass basis -r'_A=-r_w is the default, because that is what a differential reactor measures.

Why the rate depends on what it depends on

-r_A=f(C_A,T). Rate ∝ collision frequency, which needs frequency + right orientation + enough energy. Raise it by raising concentration (partial pressure) or by raising T — and temperature always dominates, through k=k_0e^{-E_A/RT}. In -r_A=kC_A^n the order n is found by experiment (and n\lt3, because three-body collisions are rare).

Ideal continuous reactors

Mixed flow (CSTR)Plug flow (PFR)
Mixing assumptionPerfect mixing at the molecular levelPerfect radial mixing, no axial (lateral) mixing
Residence timeMolecules of different residence times mix with each otherEvery molecule spends exactly the same time
Performance\dfrac{\tau}{C_{A0}}=\dfrac{V}{F_{A0}}=\dfrac{X_A}{-r_A}\dfrac{\tau}{C_{A0}}=\dfrac{V}{F_{A0}}=\displaystyle\int_0^{X}\frac{dX}{-r_A}
Three one-liners he wrote out ① Why is CSTR conversion lower than PFR? A CSTR operates entirely at the low exit concentration, so it works at the lowest rate in the whole range; the PFR sees the full concentration profile. ② PFR behaves as a CSTR at infinite recycle; adding recycle to a CSTR changes nothing, since it is already perfectly mixed. ③ Mixing and order: mixing does not affect conversion for n=1; late mixing gives higher conversion for n\gt1 (and early mixing wins for n\lt1). Whenever a quantity varies in space, you end up integrating.

Equilibrium vs steady state: equilibrium is a thermodynamic end-point with zero net reaction; steady state only means nothing changes with time — a reactor at steady state still has a net rate. Say that sentence if he asks.

01Module 1 — Catalysis & characterisation

J. M. Smith Ch 7 (heterogeneous reactions, rates) and Ch 8 (catalyst physical properties). Tutorial 1 lives here.

1.1 The vocabulary he grades on

TermOne-line answer
CatalystA substance that increases the rate by offering a path of lower activation energy; it is not consumed and cannot shift equilibrium — it speeds up forward and reverse equally.
PromoterSmall additive, itself nearly inactive, that raises activity/selectivity/stability. Structural (Al₂O₃ on Fe — stops sintering) and electronic (K₂O on Fe — tunes chemisorption) in NH₃ synthesis.
Inhibitor / negative catalystAdditive that deliberately lowers activity or suppresses an unwanted parallel reaction (improves selectivity).
PoisonImpurity that chemisorbs strongly and irreversibly on active sites (S, Pb, As on Pt). Deactivation = poisoning, fouling/coking, sintering.
Support / carrierHigh-area inert solid (γ-Al₂O₃, SiO₂, C, zeolite) that disperses the active phase and gives mechanical/thermal stability.
SelectivityRatio of desired-product formation rate to undesired; the real reason catalysts are chosen, more than activity.
Dispersion(surface metal atoms)/(total metal atoms), from chemisorption of H₂/CO — not from BET.
Physisorption vs chemisorption — a guaranteed 2 marks
PhysisorptionChemisorption
Forcevan der WaalsChemical bond (electron sharing/transfer)
Heat≈ heat of condensation, 5–40 kJ/mol40–400 kJ/mol
LayersMultilayerMonolayer only
SpecificityNon-specificHighly specific to the surface–adsorbate pair
TemperatureLow T, near the boiling point of the adsorbateWide range, often high T; may be activated
ReversibilityReadily reversibleOften irreversible
Used forTotal area (BET), pore-size distributionActive-site count, dispersion, and it is the step that makes catalysis happen

His numbers notes: \Delta H_{\text{ads}} is 0.5\text{–}5\ \mathrm{kcal/g\,mol} for physisorption (≈ heat of condensation) and 5\text{–}100\ \mathrm{kcal/g\,mol} for chemisorption (≈ a bond energy). Chemisorption is a single layer; anything beyond the first layer is physisorption. Catalysis runs on chemisorption.

1.2 BET surface area — the most-asked item in the course

Principle: multilayer physisorption of an inert gas (N₂ at its normal boiling point −195.8 °C = 77.4 K, in a liquid-N₂ bath). From the isotherm extract the volume needed for exactly one monolayer, V_m; multiply the number of molecules in it by the footprint of one molecule.

Assumptions (BET = Langmuir extended to multilayers)

  • Homogeneous surface, identical sites, no lateral interaction.
  • Infinite number of layers; a layer need not be complete before the next starts.
  • Langmuir kinetics apply to each layer (adsorption on layer i = desorption from layer i+1).
  • Heat of adsorption is E_1 for the first layer and equals the heat of liquefaction E_L for every layer above it.
\frac{P}{V(P_0-P)}=\frac{1}{V_mC}+\frac{C-1}{V_mC}\cdot\frac{P}{P_0},\qquad C\approx\exp\!\left[\frac{E_1-E_L}{RT}\right]

Plot P/[V(P_0-P)] against P/P_0; it is linear only over P/P_0 = 0.05\text{–}0.35. With slope s and intercept i:

V_m=\frac{1}{s+i},\qquad C=1+\frac{s}{i},\qquad S_g=\frac{V_m}{22414}\,N_A\,\alpha
Numbers to carry into the hall \alpha_{\mathrm{N_2}} = 16.2\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{cm^2} · \alpha_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 14.2\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{cm^2} · N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} · molar volume 22414\ \mathrm{cm^3(STP)/mol} · 10^4\ \mathrm{cm^2/g} = 1\ \mathrm{m^2/g}.
Trap When the plot axes are in g/cc (as in Tutorial 1 Q4 and Quiz 1 Q2), V_m already comes out per gram, so S_g is already specific. The sample mass is then needed only if the question says “area of the sample”. Also: s+i, never s-i.
ExBET worked in 4 lines (Quiz 1 Q2 style)

Given i = 6.5\times10^{-4} g/cc, s = 0.0756 g/cc, mass = 0.576 g, N₂ at −195.8 °C.

1 — monolayer volume
V_m=\frac{1}{s+i}=\frac{1}{0.07625}=13.11\ \mathrm{cm^3(STP)/g}
2 — molecules per gram
N=\frac{13.11}{22414}\times 6.022\times10^{23}=3.524\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{g^{-1}}
3 — area
S_g=N\alpha=3.524\times10^{20}\times16.2\times10^{-16}=5.71\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm^2/g}=57.1\ \mathrm{m^2/g}
4 — extras that fetch marks

Sample area =5.71\times10^5\times0.576=3.29\times10^5\ \mathrm{cm^2}\approx 32.9\ \mathrm{m^2}. BET constant C=1+s/i=117 — large C means strong adsorbate–adsorbent interaction, so the monolayer completes before multilayers build and the analysis is valid. 57 m²/g is a sensible alumina number.

1.3 Pore volume, densities, porosity, mean pore radius

Helium–mercury displacement: Hg does not enter pores below ~10⁴ Å at ambient pressure, He does.

\rho_p=\frac{m}{V_{\mathrm{Hg}}}\ \text{(particle/pellet density)},\qquad \rho_s=\frac{m}{V_{\mathrm{He}}}\ \text{(true/solid density)} V_g=\frac{V_{\mathrm{Hg}}-V_{\mathrm{He}}}{m}=\frac{1}{\rho_p}-\frac{1}{\rho_s},\qquad \varepsilon_p=V_g\rho_p=1-\frac{\rho_p}{\rho_s}

Assuming straight cylindrical pores of one size, equate volume and area:

\bar a=\frac{2V_g}{S_g}\quad\text{(mean pore radius)}

Pore-size distribution: mercury porosimetry for large pores (a\gt 100 Å, Washburn a=-2\sigma\cos\theta/P) and N₂ desorption/capillary condensation for small pores (Kelvin equation). The external (geometric) area of spheres:

S_x=\frac{6}{d_p}\ \left[\frac{\mathrm{cm^2}}{\mathrm{cm^3}}\right],\qquad S_g^{\text{ext}}=\frac{6}{d_p\rho_p}\ \left[\frac{\mathrm{cm^2}}{\mathrm{g}}\right]
Feel for the numbers External area of a 100 µm bead ≈ 0.04 m²/g; BET area of the same catalyst ≈ 200–1000 m²/g. Internal area beats external by ~10⁴. That single sentence answers “why porous catalysts?” and half of Module 3.

1.4 Diffusion inside pores — where Module 1 hands over to Module 3

RegimeWhenRelation
Bulk / molecularpore ≫ mean free path (high P, wide pores)D_{AB}\propto T^{3/2}/P
Knudsenpore ≲ mean free path (low P, small pores)D_K=9700\,\bar a\sqrt{T/M} cm²/s, \bar a in cm; independent of P
Combinedin between\dfrac{1}{D}=\dfrac{1}{D_{AB}}+\dfrac{1}{D_K}
Configurationalzeolite-size poresmolecule ≈ pore; activated, very small D
D_e=\frac{D\,\varepsilon_p}{\tau}\qquad (\tau\approx 2\text{–}4,\ \text{tortuosity; some texts write } D_e = D\varepsilon_p\sigma/\tau)

1.5 The seven steps of a catalytic gas–solid reaction

Intrinsic vs global rate — say this sentence The intrinsic (chemical) rate is what the surface would do at the local conditions it actually sees; the global rate is what you measure per mass of catalyst from bulk-fluid conditions. They differ whenever transport resistances are not negligible: -r_{\text{global}} = \eta\,\Omega\,(-r_{\text{intrinsic}})|_{\text{bulk}}. At steady state all seven steps carry the same flux, so resistances in series add.

1.6 Film mass transfer in series with the surface reaction notes

He derived this on the board for A(\ell)\xrightarrow{\text{cat}}B and it is the cleanest “show that” in Module 1. Assumptions: a static film of unknown thickness around the pellet, transport through it by diffusion, and the whole fluid-side resistance sitting in that film.

1 — transport of A to the surface
-r_A=k_ga\left(C_{Ab}-C_{As}\right)\qquad\text{(}k_g=\text{mass-transfer coefficient, } a=\text{interfacial area)}

We write it this way precisely because N_A=-D\,dC_A/dz is useless here — the film thickness is unknown.

2 — reaction at the surface (first order)
-r_s=k_sC_{As}\qquad (C_{As}=\text{surface concentration, not measurable})
3 — steady state: the two rates are equal, so eliminate C_{As}
k_ga\left(C_{Ab}-C_{As}\right)=k_sC_{As}\ \Longrightarrow\ C_{As}=\frac{k_gaC_{Ab}}{k_s+k_ga} \boxed{\,-r_s=\frac{k_sk_gaC_{Ab}}{k_s+k_ga}=\frac{C_{Ab}}{\dfrac{1}{k_s}+\dfrac{1}{k_ga}}\,}

The measurable bulk concentration C_{Ab} is the driving force; 1/k_s is the kinetic resistance and 1/(k_ga) the mass-transfer resistance. This is the global (extrinsic, observed) rate; -r_s=k_sC_{As} alone is the intrinsic rate.

CaseConditionWhat you see
I — kinetic / reaction controlk_ga\gg k_s, so 1/k_s\gg1/(k_ga)C_{As}\approx C_{Ab}, flat profile across the film; -r_s\approx k_sC_{Ab}; rate is independent of velocity and strongly temperature-sensitive
II — mass-transfer controlk_ga\ll k_sC_{As}\to0, steep profile; -r_s\approx k_gaC_{Ab}; rate rises with gas/liquid velocity and is weakly temperature-sensitive
IntermediatecomparableBoth terms matter — keep the full expression
Four ways to raise the observed rate notes ① raise C_{Ab}; ② raise the area a (smaller particles); ③ raise k_g — i.e. raise the Sherwood number by raising the velocity/turbulence; ④ raise k_s — i.e. raise the temperature. Note ③ helps only in Case II and ④ only in Case I: that is exactly the diagnostic experiment.

1.7 Catalyst shapes, preparation and the pressure-drop trade-off notes

ShapeCharacterApplication
SphericalLow manufacturing cost, relatively high pressure drop, large diffusion lengthHydrodesulfurisation (HDS), methanation
IrregularCloser packing ⇒ less voidage ⇒ low mass-transfer coefficient, high pressure drop, low surface areaAmmonia, formaldehyde
PelletRegular shape, good mechanical strength, low surface areaCO shift, hydrogenation
Extruded cylinder (ring, minilith, wagon-wheel)Low pressure drop, poor strength (tensile & compressive)HDS
MonolithLow pressure drop, small diffusion length, poor radial heat transferExhaust-gas cleaning

Smaller particles mean more area and a shorter diffusion path, but less voidage and therefore a bigger pressure drop — Ergun:

\frac{\Delta P}{L}=\frac{150\mu v(1-\varepsilon)^2}{d_p^2\varepsilon^3}+\frac{1.75\rho v^2(1-\varepsilon)}{d_p\varepsilon^2}

High \Delta P ⇒ a bigger pump ⇒ extra cost; but too low a rate ⇒ more catalyst ⇒ also extra cost. Shape selection is this trade-off, and that sentence is the answer to “why not simply use powder?”. Fixed bed = solids at rest; fluidised bed = solids in movement.

Preparation — the generic route

  • Precipitation example: \mathrm{Al(NO_3)_3}+\mathrm{NH_4OH}\rightarrow\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}+\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}.
  • Sol–gel: ① precipitation of a liquid suspension by hydrolysis of a precursor salt, ② condensation to a gel.
  • Catalyst classes: metals (Fe, Cu, Pt, Pd, Rh), semiconductors (NiO, ZnO), insulators (Al₂O₃, SiO₂); supports also include SiC and carbon. Unsupported example: Fe for NH₃; supported example: V₂O₅/SiO₂ for \mathrm{SO_2\rightarrow SO_3}.

Two numbers that measure “how good”

\text{TOF}=\frac{\text{moles of reactant converted per unit time}}{\text{moles of active sites}}\ \left[\mathrm{s^{-1}}\right],\ \ \text{typically }10^{-4}\text{–}10^{4} \text{Dispersion}=\frac{\text{number of surface metal atoms}}{\text{total number of metal atoms}}\times100\%

Both need the active-site count, so both come from chemisorption, never from BET.

IUPAC pore classification

ClassSizeConsequence
Micropored_p\lt2 nmConfigurational / Knudsen transport; zeolites
Mesopore2\ \text{nm}\lt d_p\lt50\ \text{nm}Knudsen; where most BET area lives; capillary condensation
Macropored_p\gt50 nmBulk diffusion; the “highways” feeding the mesopores

Typical catalyst particle sizes run 50 µm to 3000 µm; pore sizes are of the order of ångströms. Physisorption gives you surface area + pore volume; chemisorption gives you active sites.

02Module 2 — Adsorption & LHHW rate laws

Fogler Ch 10 up to §10.4.4. This is the heart of the paper — Tutorial 3 was entirely this. Learn the algorithm, not the individual answers.

2.1 Isotherms

Langmuir — monolayer, fixed number of identical sites, one molecule per site, heat of adsorption independent of coverage, no interaction between adsorbed molecules, dynamic equilibrium.

r_{\text{ads}}=k_aP(1-\theta),\quad r_{\text{des}}=k_d\theta\ \Longrightarrow\ \boxed{\ \theta=\frac{KP}{1+KP}\ },\quad K=\frac{k_a}{k_d} q=\frac{q_{\max}KP}{1+KP}\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{P}{q}=\frac{1}{q_{\max}K}+\frac{P}{q_{\max}}\quad\text{(plot } P/q \text{ vs } P\text{)}

Limits: KP\ll1\Rightarrow\theta\approx KP (first order, Henry’s law); KP\gg1\Rightarrow\theta\to1 (saturated, zero order).

IsothermExpressionSay this about it
Langmuir\theta=\dfrac{KP}{1+KP}Monolayer, uniform sites. Basis of every LHHW rate law.
Dissociative\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{KP}}{1+\sqrt{KP}}A₂ + 2S ⇌ 2A·S. Square root = two sites. (Tut 2 Q1: H₂, N₂ on Fe.)
Competitive\theta_i=\dfrac{K_iP_i}{1+\sum_j K_jP_j}All species fight for the same sites — this sum is the LHHW denominator.
BETsee Module 1Langmuir relaxed to infinite layers; used for area, not for kinetics.
Freundlichq=K_FP^{1/n}Empirical; heterogeneous surface, heat of adsorption falls logarithmically with coverage. No saturation limit.
Temkin\theta=\dfrac{RT}{b}\ln(K P)Heat of adsorption falls linearly with coverage.
Tóth Tut 2\theta=\dfrac{Kp}{\left[1+(Kp)^{n}\right]^{1/n}}Langmuir + heterogeneity parameter n; n=1 gives back Langmuir.
Multi-site Langmuir Tut 2\dfrac{q}{q_{\max}}=Kp\left(1-\dfrac{q}{q_{\max}}\right)^{a}One molecule occupies a sites.
van ’t Hoff — the Tutorial-2 tail \ln K = -\dfrac{\Delta H_{\text{ads}}}{RT}+\text{const}. Plot \ln K vs 1/T; slope =-\Delta H_{\text{ads}}/R. Adsorption is exothermic, so \Delta H_{\text{ads}}\lt0, K falls as T rises. (Physisorption ≈ −20 kJ/mol; chemisorption ≈ −100 kJ/mol or more.)
Linearise everything — he drilled this notes
IsothermPlotSlope / intercept
Langmuir (volume form)\dfrac{1}{V} vs \dfrac{1}{p}slope =\dfrac{1}{V_mK}, intercept =\dfrac{1}{V_m}
Langmuir (site form)\dfrac{p}{C_{A\cdot S}} vs pslope =\dfrac{1}{C_t}, intercept =\dfrac{1}{K_AC_t}
Dissociative\dfrac{\sqrt{p}}{C_{A\cdot S}} vs \sqrt{p}slope =\dfrac{2}{C_t}, intercept =\dfrac{1}{C_t\sqrt{K_A}}
BET\dfrac{P}{V(P_0-P)} vs \dfrac{P}{P_0}V_m=\dfrac{1}{s+i}, C=1+\dfrac{s}{i}
van ’t Hoff\ln K vs \dfrac{1}{T}slope =-\dfrac{\Delta H}{R}, intercept =\dfrac{\Delta S}{R}
A family of \theta-vs-p curves at T_1\lt T_2\lt T_3\lt T_4 fans downwards as T rises, because K falls — that sketch is worth drawing if he asks about temperature.
Where each isotherm comes from notes Langmuir assumes \Delta H_{\text{ads}} is independent of coverage. Relax that one assumption two ways and you get the other two: Temkin takes \Delta H_{\text{ads}}\propto1/\theta giving \theta=k_1\ln(k_2p); Freundlich takes \Delta H_{\text{ads}}(\theta)=\Delta H_0\ln\theta giving \theta=c\,p^{1/n} with n\gt1. Relax “monolayer” instead and you get BET.

2.2 The three elementary steps, written properly

C_v = vacant sites, C_{i\cdot S} = sites holding i, C_t = total sites. Every step is written as forward − reverse.

StepNet rate
Adsorption A+S\rightleftharpoons A\!\cdot\!Sr_{AD}=k_A\!\left(p_AC_v-\dfrac{C_{A\cdot S}}{K_A}\right)
Dissociative A_2+2S\rightleftharpoons 2A\!\cdot\!Sr_{AD}=k_A\!\left(p_{A_2}C_v^2-\dfrac{C_{A\cdot S}^2}{K_A}\right)
Surface rxn, single site A\!\cdot\!S\rightleftharpoons B\!\cdot\!Sr_S=k_S\!\left(C_{A\cdot S}-\dfrac{C_{B\cdot S}}{K_S}\right)
Surface rxn, dual site A\!\cdot\!S+S\rightleftharpoons B\!\cdot\!S+Sr_S=k_S\!\left(C_{A\cdot S}C_v-\dfrac{C_{B\cdot S}C_v}{K_S}\right)
Langmuir–Hinshelwood A\!\cdot\!S+B\!\cdot\!S\rightleftharpoons C\!\cdot\!S+Sr_S=k_S\!\left(C_{A\cdot S}C_{B\cdot S}-\dfrac{C_{C\cdot S}C_v}{K_S}\right)
Eley–Rideal A\!\cdot\!S+B(g)\rightarrow C\!\cdot\!Sr_S=k_S\,C_{A\cdot S}\,p_B
Desorption B\!\cdot\!S\rightleftharpoons B+Sr_D=k_D\!\left(C_{B\cdot S}-\dfrac{p_BC_v}{K_{D_B}}\right),\ \ K_{D_B}=\dfrac{1}{K_B}
Site balanceC_t=C_v+\sum_i C_{i\cdot S}

2.3 The algorithm — write these five lines, every time

  1. Postulate a mechanism (adsorption / surface reaction / desorption) and pick the rate-limiting step (RLS).
  2. Write the rate of the RLS only, in terms of surface concentrations.
  3. Set every other step at quasi-equilibrium (its rate ≈ 0, i.e. r_i/k_i\to0) and solve each for its coverage in terms of p_i and C_v.
  4. Use the site balance to eliminate C_v.
  5. Lump k_SC_t (or k_SC_t^2) into a single k. Check the reversible form vanishes at equilibrium.
General LHHW shape -r'_A=\frac{(\text{kinetic term})\times(\text{driving force})}{(\text{adsorption term})^{\,n}} n = number of sites involved in the rate-limiting step. Driving force =\left(p_A-\dfrac{p_B}{K_P}\right) for a reversible reaction, =p_A if irreversible. A species appears in the denominator only if it adsorbs.
Two framings he used in class notes Resistances in series. Adsorption, surface reaction and desorption behave like R_{AD}, R_S, R_D in series across one battery: I=V/\sum R. If \sum R=100 with R_1=99 and R_2=R_3=0.5, step 1 is the rate. That is what “rate-limiting step” means, and why the denominator is called the resistance term and the numerator the driving force.

PSSH. Pseudo-steady-state hypothesis: the surface intermediates are present in vanishing amounts and at a steady level, C_{T\cdot S},C_{B\cdot S}\approx0 and r_{T\cdot S}\approx r_{B\cdot S}\approx0. Operationally you set r_i/k_i\to0 for every non-limiting step — which is exactly step 3 of the algorithm above.

2.4 The limiting-case table (Fogler Table 10-5 = Tutorial 3 Q1)

Mechanism, surface reaction limitingRate lawSignature
Single site A\!\cdot\!S\to B\!\cdot\!S-r'_A=\dfrac{kp_A}{1+K_Ap_A+K_Bp_B}Denominator power 1
Dual site A\!\cdot\!S+S\to B\!\cdot\!S+S-r'_A=\dfrac{kp_A}{(1+K_Ap_A+K_Bp_B)^2}Power 2 from the extra C_v
Dual site A\!\cdot\!S+B\!\cdot\!S\to C\!\cdot\!S+S-r'_A=\dfrac{kp_Ap_B}{(1+K_Ap_A+K_Bp_B+K_Cp_C)^2}Both reactants adsorbed → product of pressures on top
Eley–Rideal A\!\cdot\!S+B(g)\to C\!\cdot\!S-r'_A=\dfrac{kp_Ap_B}{1+K_Ap_A+K_Cp_C}No K_Bp_B in the denominator — B never adsorbs
Adsorption of A limiting-r'_A=\dfrac{k\left(p_A-p_B/K_P\right)}{1+K_Bp_B\ (+\dots)}K_Ap_A is absent from the denominator; rate ≈ first order in A at low p_A
Desorption of B limiting-r'_A=\dfrac{k\left(p_A-p_B/K_P\right)}{ \dots+K_AK_Sp_A}p_A appears in the denominator, so the rate levels off / falls as p_A rises
Three traps that cost whole questions ① The exponent of the denominator counts sites in the RLS, not species in the reaction. ② A product that does not adsorb contributes nothing to the denominator — do not add it “to be safe”. ③ For dissociative adsorption the coverage carries a \sqrt{\ } and the site balance gets 2\sqrt{K p} terms (Tut 2 Q1).
DerivationDual-site, surface-reaction limited — the full 6 lines he wants

Mechanism: A+S\rightleftharpoons A\!\cdot\!S; A\!\cdot\!S+S\rightleftharpoons B\!\cdot\!S+S (slow); B\!\cdot\!S\rightleftharpoons B+S.

1 — rate of the RLS
-r'_A=k_S\left(C_{A\cdot S}C_v-\frac{C_{B\cdot S}C_v}{K_S}\right)
2 — the other steps are at equilibrium
C_{A\cdot S}=K_Ap_AC_v,\qquad C_{B\cdot S}=K_Bp_BC_v
3 — substitute
-r'_A=k_SC_v^2\left(K_Ap_A-\frac{K_Bp_B}{K_S}\right)=k_SK_AC_v^2\left(p_A-\frac{p_B}{K_P}\right),\quad K_P=\frac{K_AK_S}{K_B}
4 — site balance
C_t=C_v+C_{A\cdot S}+C_{B\cdot S}=C_v\left(1+K_Ap_A+K_Bp_B\right)\ \Rightarrow\ C_v=\frac{C_t}{1+K_Ap_A+K_Bp_B}
5 — combine and lump k=k_SK_AC_t^2
\boxed{\,-r'_A=\frac{k\left(p_A-p_B/K_P\right)}{\left(1+K_Ap_A+K_Bp_B\right)^2}\,}
6 — check

At equilibrium p_A=p_B/K_P and the rate vanishes. If the slow step had been single-site (A\!\cdot\!S\rightleftharpoons B\!\cdot\!S) there is no extra C_v, and the denominator is raised to the power 1 — that is exactly Tutorial 3, Q2(i) vs Q2(ii) for n-pentene ⇌ i-pentene over alumina.

2.5 Deducing the rate law from data (Fogler §10.4 = Tutorial 3 Q6)

Toluene + H₂ → benzene + methane on silica-alumina in a differential reactor (so measured rate ≈ point rate at the stated pressures).

ObservationDataConclusion
p_{H_2}:1\to2\to471.8 → 142 → 284First order in H₂ ⇒ p_{H_2} in the numerator, not in the denominator
p_T:0.5\to1\to5\to2047 → 71.8 → 117 → 133Rate rises then saturates ⇒ toluene adsorbs; K_Tp_T in the denominator
p_B:0\to1\to4\to571.8 → 41.6 → 19.7 → 17.1Benzene inhibits ⇒ K_Bp_B in the denominator
p_M:0\to471 → 71.3Methane does not adsorb ⇒ no methane term
-r'_T=\frac{k\,p_Tp_{H_2}}{1+K_Bp_B+K_Tp_T}\quad\xrightarrow{\ \text{regression}\ }\quad -r'_T=\frac{8.7\times10^{-4}\,p_Tp_{H_2}}{1+1.39\,p_B+1.038\,p_T}\ \frac{\mathrm{mol\ T}}{\mathrm{g_{cat}\!\cdot\! s}}

Mechanism that matches: T+S\rightleftharpoons T\!\cdot\!S; B+S\rightleftharpoons B\!\cdot\!S; and the slow step T\!\cdot\!S+H_2(g)\to B\!\cdot\!S+M(g) — an Eley–Rideal step (H₂ from the gas phase), denominator power 1, methane absent from the site balance.

Two traps from Tutorial 3 Q6 The table symbol p_H means “partial pressure of H₂”, i.e. p_{H_2} — not p_{H_2}^2; if you square it, runs 7–9 cannot fit. And the tabulated rates are \times10^{-10}: rescale before quoting k.

2.6 Cumene cracking — picking the rate-limiting step from initial-rate data notes

This is the worked example he spent two lectures on (Fogler §10.3–10.4). Cumene cracks on Pt at 500 °C, 10 bar:

\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2}\ (C)\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{C_6H_6}\ (B)\ +\ \mathrm{C_3H_6}\ (P)

Mechanism: adsorption C+S\rightleftharpoons C\!\cdot\!S; surface reaction C\!\cdot\!S\rightleftharpoons B\!\cdot\!S+P(g); desorption B\!\cdot\!S\rightleftharpoons B+S. At steady state -r'_C=r_{AD}=r_S=r_D. Work each case by setting r_i/k_i\to0 for the two fast steps:

If the limiting step is…Rate lawInitial rate -r_{C0} vs p_{C0} (with p_B=p_P\approx0)
Adsorption of C-r'_C=\dfrac{C_tk_A\left(p_C-\dfrac{p_Bp_P}{K_P}\right)}{1+K_Bp_B+\dfrac{K_Bp_Bp_P}{K_S}}-r_{C0}=C_tk_Ap_C — a straight line through the origin, slope C_tk_A
Surface reaction-r'_C=\dfrac{k\left(p_C-\dfrac{p_Bp_P}{K_P}\right)}{1+K_Bp_B+K_Cp_C}-r_{C0}=\dfrac{kp_C}{1+K_Cp_C} — rises then saturates at k/K_C
Desorption of B-r'_C=\dfrac{k_DK_CK_SC_t\left(p_C-\dfrac{p_Bp_P}{K_P}\right)}{p_P+K_CK_Sp_C+K_Cp_Cp_P}-r_{C0} is independent of p_{C0} — a horizontal line
The four-step method he wrote out ① Perform the experiment (differential reactor / initial rates). ② Assume a rate law, i.e. pick a rate-limiting step. ③ Deduce the parameters by fitting. ④ If it fits, use it for reactor design; if it does not fit, go back to ②. Say this loop out loud in any “how would you establish the kinetics” answer.

2.7 Temperature — the classic “explain why” question

k rises with T (Arrhenius) while every adsorption constant K_i falls (exothermic adsorption). So at high enough T the denominator → 1 and the LHHW law degenerates into a simple power-law rate. This also makes the apparent activation energy E_{\text{app}}=E_{\text{true}}+\sum\Delta H_{\text{ads},i}, which can even come out negative if adsorption is strongly exothermic.

03Module 3 — Pore diffusion, \Phi and \eta

Levenspiel Ch 18 up to §18.3 (+ Fogler §15.1–15.3.1). He said: skip the solution of the ODE, know the formulation, the Thiele modulus and the effectiveness factor.

3.1 Formulation — the shell balance (know how to set it up)

Steady state, isothermal pellet, first-order reaction, diffusion described by an effective diffusivity D_e. Over a shell of a slab of half-thickness L:

\underbrace{\left(D_eA\frac{dC_A}{dx}\right)_{x+\Delta x}-\left(D_eA\frac{dC_A}{dx}\right)_{x}}_{\text{diffusion in}-\text{out}}\;-\;\underbrace{kC_A\,A\,\Delta x}_{\text{consumed}}=0 \Rightarrow\quad D_e\frac{d^2C_A}{dx^2}-kC_A=0\qquad\text{(sphere: }\frac{D_e}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\!\left(r^2\frac{dC_A}{dr}\right)-kC_A=0)

Boundary conditions: C_A=C_{As} at the outer surface; dC_A/dx=0 at the centre (symmetry / no flux). Non-dimensionalising with \psi=C_A/C_{As}, \lambda=x/L gives d^2\psi/d\lambda^2=\Phi^2\psi — and the group that pops out is the Thiele modulus.

Definitions — the two you must not confuse \Phi\ (\text{or }M_T)=L\sqrt{\frac{k}{D_e}}=\sqrt{\frac{\text{surface reaction rate}}{\text{diffusion rate}}},\qquad L=\frac{V_p}{S_x}\ \left(\text{slab }L,\ \text{cylinder }\frac{R}{2},\ \text{sphere }\frac{R}{3}\right) \eta=\frac{\text{actual rate with pore diffusion}}{\text{rate if the whole interior were at }C_{As}}=\frac{-r_{A,\text{obs}}}{-r_A(C_{As})}\quad\Rightarrow\quad -r_{A,\text{obs}}=\eta\,k\,C_{As} Fogler writes the sphere modulus on the radius: \phi_1=R\sqrt{k\rho_cS_a/D_e}=3\,M_T. State which definition you are using.

3.2 The results (no ODE solving needed)

\text{slab (Levenspiel, }L=V_p/S_x):\quad \eta=\frac{\tanh M_T}{M_T};\qquad \text{sphere (Fogler): }\ \eta=\frac{3}{\phi_1^2}\left(\phi_1\coth\phi_1-1\right)
RegimeCriterionBehaviour
Reaction (kinetic) controlM_T\lt0.4  (\phi_1\lt1)\eta\to1; concentration nearly flat inside the pellet; whole pellet used
Intermediate0.4\lt M_T\lt4Use the full formula or the chart
Strong pore-diffusion controlM_T\gt4  (\phi_1\gt10)\eta\approx\dfrac{1}{M_T}=\dfrac{3}{\phi_1}; reaction confined to a thin outer shell

3.3 Weisz–Prater — the test you can actually run

You cannot compute \Phi without k, which is what you are trying to measure. So use the observable modulus (all quantities measured):

C_{WP}=\eta\,\phi_1^2=\frac{\left(-r'_{A,\text{obs}}\right)\rho_cR^2}{D_eC_{As}}\qquad\left(\text{Levenspiel: } M_W=\eta M_T^2=\frac{\left(-r'''_{A,\text{obs}}\right)L^2}{D_eC_{As}}\right)
ValueVerdict
C_{WP}\ll1 (< 0.3, or M_W\lt0.15)No internal diffusion limitation — \eta\approx1, measured kinetics are true kinetics
C_{WP}\gg1 (> 6, or M_W\gt4)Severe pore-diffusion limitation — kinetics are falsified

For the external film use the Mears criterion: \dfrac{(-r'_A)\rho_bRn}{k_cC_{Ab}}\lt0.15 ⇒ external mass transfer can be ignored.

3.4 Falsified kinetics — the favourite conceptual question

In strong pore diffusion the measured rate is \eta kC_{As}\approx\frac{1}{L}\sqrt{D_ek}\,C_{As}, so it goes as \sqrt{k}:

QuantityNo diffusion limitationStrong pore diffusion
Reaction ordernn_{\text{obs}}=\dfrac{n+1}{2}  (1 → 1, 2 → 1.5, 0 → 0.5)
Activation energyEE_{\text{obs}}=\dfrac{E}{2} (since k_{\text{obs}}\propto\sqrt{kD_e})
Particle sizerate independent of d_prate \propto 1/L\propto 1/d_p
Fluid velocityno effect (that is the film test)no effect
Diagnostic in one line Change the particle size → rate changes ⇒ pore diffusion matters. Change the flow rate at fixed W/F_{A0} → rate changes ⇒ the external film matters. Neither changes anything ⇒ you are measuring true kinetics.

3.5 Putting the film back (Levenspiel §18.3)

At steady state the same flux crosses the film and is consumed inside, so the resistances add in series. For a first-order reaction on a pellet of external area S_x and volume V_p:

-r'''_A=\frac{C_{Ag}}{\dfrac{1}{k_g\left(S_x/V_p\right)}+\dfrac{1}{\eta k}}\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{1}{k_{\text{obs}}}=\underbrace{\frac{1}{k_g\,a}}_{\text{film}}+\underbrace{\frac{1}{\eta k}}_{\text{pore + surface}}

Consequences worth a mark each: the film resistance makes the surface concentration C_{As}\lt C_{Ag}, so always define \eta on C_{As}; the slowest resistance controls; film control gives an apparent first-order behaviour and a strong dependence on gas velocity.

3.6 Using it in a reactor

Once you have the global rate -r'_A=\eta\,(-r'_{A,\text{intrinsic}}), the packed-bed design equation is unchanged from CRE-I:

\frac{W}{F_{A0}}=\int_0^{X}\frac{dX}{-r'_A}\quad\text{(plug flow)},\qquad \frac{W}{F_{A0}}=\frac{X}{-r'_A\big|_{\text{exit}}}\quad\text{(mixed flow)}

Small pellets raise \eta but raise the pressure drop; that trade-off is the standard one-line answer to “how would you improve the reactor?”.

04Formula sheet — read twice, out loud

If you only have five minutes left, read this section and nothing else.

Modules 0–1

(-r_v)V=(-r_w)W=(-r_s)S;\quad \frac{V}{F_{A0}}=\frac{X}{-r_A}\ \text{(CSTR)},\quad \frac{V}{F_{A0}}=\int_0^X\frac{dX}{-r_A}\ \text{(PFR)} -r_s=\frac{C_{Ab}}{\dfrac{1}{k_s}+\dfrac{1}{k_ga}};\qquad \frac{\Delta P}{L}=\frac{150\mu v(1-\varepsilon)^2}{d_p^2\varepsilon^3}+\frac{1.75\rho v^2(1-\varepsilon)}{d_p\varepsilon^2}

Module 1

\frac{P}{V(P_0-P)}=\frac{1}{V_mC}+\frac{C-1}{V_mC}\frac{P}{P_0};\quad V_m=\frac{1}{s+i};\quad C=1+\frac{s}{i};\quad S_g=\frac{V_m}{22414}N_A\alpha \rho_p=\frac{m}{V_{\mathrm{Hg}}};\quad \rho_s=\frac{m}{V_{\mathrm{He}}};\quad V_g=\frac1{\rho_p}-\frac1{\rho_s};\quad \varepsilon_p=V_g\rho_p;\quad \bar a=\frac{2V_g}{S_g} S_x=\frac{6}{d_p};\quad S_g^{\text{ext}}=\frac{6}{d_p\rho_p};\quad D_K=9700\,\bar a\sqrt{T/M};\quad \frac1D=\frac1{D_{AB}}+\frac1{D_K};\quad D_e=\frac{D\varepsilon_p}{\tau}

\theta=\frac{KP}{1+KP};\quad \theta_{\text{diss}}=\frac{\sqrt{KP}}{1+\sqrt{KP}};\quad \theta_i=\frac{K_iP_i}{1+\sum K_jP_j};\quad \frac{P}{q}=\frac{1}{q_{\max}K}+\frac{P}{q_{\max}} -r'_A=\frac{(\text{kinetic})(\text{driving force})}{(\text{adsorption term})^{\,n}};\quad C_t=C_v+\sum C_{i\cdot S};\quad \ln K=-\frac{\Delta H_{\text{ads}}}{RT}+c \text{dual site: }\frac{k(p_A-p_B/K_P)}{(1+K_Ap_A+K_Bp_B)^2};\qquad \text{Eley–Rideal: }\frac{kp_Ap_B}{1+K_Ap_A+K_Cp_C}

Constants N_A=6.022\times10^{23} · R=8.314\ \mathrm{J/mol\,K}=1.987\ \mathrm{cal/mol\,K}=82.06\ \mathrm{cm^3atm/mol\,K} · 22414\ \mathrm{cm^3/mol} at STP · \alpha_{N_2}=16.2\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm{cm^2}, \alpha_{O_2}=14.2\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm{cm^2} · N₂ b.p. -195.8^\circ\mathrm{C}=77.4\ \mathrm{K} · 1 µm =10^{-4} cm · 1 Å =10^{-8} cm · 10^4\ \mathrm{cm^2/g}=1\ \mathrm{m^2/g}.

05Four worked problems in his style

Try each for 30 seconds before opening it. These are the four shapes a numerical can take.

W1Pore properties → effective diffusivity

Q. An alumina catalyst has V_g=0.45\ \mathrm{cm^3/g}, S_g=200\ \mathrm{m^2/g}, \rho_p=1.2\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}. Find the porosity, the mean pore radius, and D_e for N₂ at 573 K (Knudsen controlling, \tau=3).

porosity
\varepsilon_p=V_g\rho_p=0.45\times1.2=0.54
mean pore radius (cylindrical-pore model)
\bar a=\frac{2V_g}{S_g}=\frac{2(0.45)}{2\times10^{6}}=4.5\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm}=45\ \text{Å}
Knudsen diffusivity
D_K=9700\,\bar a\sqrt{T/M}=9700(4.5\times10^{-7})\sqrt{573/28}=9700(4.5\times10^{-7})(4.52)=1.97\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}
effective diffusivity
D_e=\frac{D_K\varepsilon_p}{\tau}=\frac{1.97\times10^{-2}\times0.54}{3}=3.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}
Answer\varepsilon_p=0.54, \bar a=45 Å, D_e=3.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}. A 45 Å pore is far smaller than the mean free path at 1 atm, which justifies treating the transport as Knudsen.
W2Thiele modulus, effectiveness factor and Weisz–Prater

Q. Spherical pellets, d_p=0.6 cm, first-order k=2\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} (per cm³ of pellet), D_e=3.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm^2/s}. Find \eta and decide whether pore diffusion matters.

characteristic length
L=\frac{V_p}{S_x}=\frac{\tfrac43\pi R^3}{4\pi R^2}=\frac{R}{3}=\frac{0.3}{3}=0.1\ \mathrm{cm}
Thiele modulus
M_T=L\sqrt{\frac{k}{D_e}}=0.1\sqrt{\frac{2}{3.6\times10^{-3}}}=0.1\times23.6=2.36\quad(\phi_1=3M_T=7.1)
effectiveness factor
\eta=\frac{\tanh M_T}{M_T}=\frac{\tanh 2.36}{2.36}=\frac{0.982}{2.36}=0.42

Exact sphere formula: \eta=\dfrac{3}{\phi_1^2}(\phi_1\coth\phi_1-1)=\dfrac{3}{50.4}(7.1-1)=0.36. Quote whichever the question’s book uses and say so; they agree to ~15 % here and merge onto \eta\approx1/M_T=3/\phi_1=0.42 at large \Phi.

observable check
C_{WP}=\eta\phi_1^2=0.36\times50.4\approx18\ \gg 6
Answer\eta\approx0.4: only about 40 % of the catalyst is being used, and C_{WP}\gg6 confirms strong pore-diffusion control. Halving the pellet diameter halves M_T and roughly doubles the rate per gram.
W3Diagnosing falsified kinetics from data

Q. On 6 mm pellets the measured order is 1.5 and E_{\text{obs}}=42\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}. When the pellets are crushed to 1 mm the rate per gram rises sharply, then stops changing on further crushing. Interpret.

  • The rate depends on particle size ⇒ pore diffusion was limiting on the 6 mm pellets (\text{rate}\propto1/d_p).
  • Crushing further changes nothing ⇒ at 1 mm, \eta\approx1, so those data are true kinetics.
  • Falsified values: n_{\text{obs}}=(n+1)/2=1.5\Rightarrow n_{\text{true}}=2; E_{\text{obs}}=E/2\Rightarrow E_{\text{true}}\approx84\ \mathrm{kJ/mol}.
  • Had the rate instead responded to gas velocity, the film would have been the culprit — check with the Mears criterion.
Answer6 mm data are diffusion-falsified (n_{\text{true}}=2, E_{\text{true}}\approx84 kJ/mol); 1 mm data are intrinsic. Design with the intrinsic kinetics plus an \eta computed for the pellet size you actually use.
W4“Show that…” — dissociative adsorption (Tutorial 2 Q1)

Q. H₂ and N₂ both chemisorb dissociatively on Fe. Show that C_{N\cdot S}=\dfrac{C_t\sqrt{K_{N_2}p_{N_2}}}{1+2\sqrt{K_{N_2}p_{N_2}}+2\sqrt{K_{H_2}p_{H_2}}}.

1 — equilibria
N_2+2S\rightleftharpoons 2N\!\cdot\!S:\quad K_{N_2}=\frac{C_{N\cdot S}^2}{p_{N_2}C_v^2}\ \Rightarrow\ C_{N\cdot S}=C_v\sqrt{K_{N_2}p_{N_2}} \text{likewise}\quad C_{H\cdot S}=C_v\sqrt{K_{H_2}p_{H_2}}
2 — site balance (each dissociated atom occupies one site, and there are two of them)
C_t=C_v+C_{N\cdot S}+C_{H\cdot S}\ \text{per atom}\ \Rightarrow\ C_t=C_v\left(1+2\sqrt{K_{N_2}p_{N_2}}+2\sqrt{K_{H_2}p_{H_2}}\right)
3 — eliminate C_v
C_{N\cdot S}=\frac{C_t\sqrt{K_{N_2}p_{N_2}}}{1+2\sqrt{K_{N_2}p_{N_2}}+2\sqrt{K_{H_2}p_{H_2}}}
The point of the questionThe factor 2 comes from one molecule producing two adsorbed atoms; the square root is the fingerprint of dissociative adsorption. Any rate law built on this step will show \sqrt{p} dependence at low coverage.

06Twelve traps

  1. Roll-number digits. Write “x = _, y = _, z = _” as the very first line and box it. Re-read which digit goes where — 0.xy vs 0.yzx are different numbers.
  2. BET: V_m=1/(s+i), not 1/s. And C=1+s/i.
  3. Units: µm → cm is \times10^{-4}; Å → cm is \times10^{-8}; m²/g → cm²/g is \times10^{4}.
  4. BET measures total area; chemisorption measures active sites. Never swap them.
  5. Denominator exponent = number of sites in the rate-limiting step.
  6. Non-adsorbing species get no denominator term (Eley–Rideal, methane in the toluene problem).
  7. Reversible reactions: the numerator must be (p_A-p_B/K_P) so the rate vanishes at equilibrium — state that check.
  8. Dissociative adsorption ⇒ \sqrt{Kp} and a factor 2 in the site balance.
  9. Thiele modulus: Levenspiel uses L=V_p/S_x=R/3; Fogler uses R. \phi_1=3M_T. Declare your definition.
  10. η is defined on the surface concentration C_{As}, not the bulk C_{Ag} — that is what lets you add the film resistance in series.
  11. Falsified kinetics: E is halved, the order moves towards 1 — (n+1)/2, so a zero-order reaction looks half-order and a second-order one looks 1.5.
  12. A catalyst never changes equilibrium conversion. If a question tempts you there, say so explicitly — it is a free mark.
  13. Rate basis. Check whether the question wants per volume, per gram or per m² before you substitute: (-r_v)V=(-r_w)W=(-r_s)S. Differential-reactor data are per gram.
  14. Initial-rate shapes. Linear in p ⇒ adsorption limiting; saturating ⇒ surface reaction; flat ⇒ desorption. Sketch the curve, don’t just assert.
  15. His units for heats of adsorption are kcal/g·mol (0.5–5 physisorption, 5–100 chemisorption). Quote them in his units, and note that adsorption is exothermic.

07Rapid-fire — 28 answers

Tap to reveal. Anything you miss, scroll back to that section right away.

1Why is N₂ at 77 K used for BET?
It physisorbs weakly and non-specifically on every surface, its cross-sectional area (16.2 Å²) is well established, and at its boiling point P_0 is conveniently ~1 atm so the useful range P/P_0=0.05\text{–}0.35 is easy to cover.
2Why is the BET plot linear only for P/P_0=0.05\text{–}0.35?
Below 0.05 surface heterogeneity and the strongest sites dominate (the uniform-site assumption fails); above 0.35 capillary condensation in pores makes the uptake exceed what multilayer BET predicts.
3What does a large BET constant C mean?
C\approx\exp[(E_1-E_L)/RT]: a large C means the first layer is bound far more strongly than the liquid, so the monolayer completes cleanly before multilayers begin — BET is reliable.
4Physical meaning of the Thiele modulus?
The ratio of the intrinsic surface-reaction rate to the pore-diffusion rate. Large \Phi ⇒ reaction consumes the reactant faster than diffusion can supply the interior.
5Physical meaning of \eta?
Actual rate ÷ the rate that would occur if the entire interior were at the external surface concentration. \eta=1 means the whole pellet is fully used.
6Can \eta exceed 1?
Not for an isothermal, positive-order reaction. It can for a strongly exothermic non-isothermal pellet (the interior gets hotter) or for negative-order kinetics — outside our scope, but worth one sentence.
7Why define L=V_p/S_x?
With that length the \eta–\Phi curves for slab, cylinder and sphere nearly collapse onto one curve, so a single chart serves all pellet shapes.
8How do you know pore diffusion is limiting without knowing k?
Use the Weisz–Prater number C_{WP}=(-r'_{\text{obs}})\rho_cR^2/(D_eC_{As}) — every quantity is measurable. \lt0.3 negligible, \gt6 severe.
9Difference between intrinsic and global rate?
Intrinsic = chemistry alone at the local conditions; global = measured per mass of catalyst from bulk conditions, i.e. chemistry × all transport resistances (\eta and the film).
10What does the exponent on the LHHW denominator tell you?
The number of catalytic sites participating in the rate-limiting step — 1 for single-site or Eley–Rideal, 2 for dual-site.
11Langmuir–Hinshelwood vs Eley–Rideal?
LH: both reactants are adsorbed and react site-to-site (both appear in the denominator). ER: an adsorbed species reacts with a molecule striking from the gas phase (the gas species appears only in the numerator).
12Product inhibition in a rate law — what does it look like and why?
A K_Pp_P term in the denominator: the product occupies sites and reduces C_v. Benzene in the toluene hydrodealkylation is the standard example.
13Why does K fall with temperature?
Adsorption is exothermic (\Delta H_{\text{ads}}\lt0), so by van ’t Hoff K decreases as T rises; at high T the denominator → 1 and the LHHW law becomes a power law.
14Promoter vs support vs poison in one line each?
Promoter: inactive additive that boosts activity/selectivity/stability (Al₂O₃, K₂O on Fe). Support: high-area carrier that disperses and stabilises the active phase. Poison: impurity that irreversibly blocks active sites (S on Pt).
15Which step is usually assumed rate-limiting, and why is that assumption made?
The surface reaction, because adsorption and desorption are usually fast. It is an assumption — you validate it by checking that the resulting rate law fits the pressure dependences of the data.
16A rate law fits the data. Does that prove the mechanism?
No. Several mechanisms produce the same algebraic form (Fogler P10-3). A rate law can only disprove mechanisms; supporting evidence needs spectroscopy, isotope labelling, independent adsorption measurements.
17How do you measure pore volume and porosity?
He–Hg displacement: V_g=1/\rho_p-1/\rho_s, \varepsilon_p=V_g\rho_p. Mercury does not penetrate small pores at ambient pressure; helium does.
18When is Knudsen diffusion dominant?
When the pore radius is smaller than the mean free path — small pores, low pressure. Then D_K=9700\bar a\sqrt{T/M}, independent of pressure and proportional to pore size.
19Strong pore diffusion: how do order, E and particle size behave?
n_{\text{obs}}=(n+1)/2, E_{\text{obs}}=E/2, and the rate per gram \propto1/d_p.
20Why is a porous catalyst used at all, given that pore diffusion hurts?
Internal area exceeds external area by about four orders of magnitude (≈ 200 m²/g vs ≈ 0.04 m²/g), so even \eta=0.1 leaves the porous pellet enormously more productive than a non-porous one of the same size.
21Three ways of writing the rate — and the link between them? notes
Per reactor volume, per mass of catalyst, per catalyst surface: (-r_v)V=(-r_w)W=(-r_s)S. Heterogeneous kinetics default to the mass basis because that is what a differential reactor gives.
22Derive the global rate when a film resistance sits in series with a first-order surface reaction. notes
Equate k_ga(C_{Ab}-C_{As})=k_sC_{As}, eliminate the unmeasurable C_{As}, and get -r_s=C_{Ab}/\left(1/k_s+1/(k_ga)\right): driving force over the sum of the kinetic and mass-transfer resistances.
23How do you tell film control from kinetic control experimentally? notes
Raise the velocity (Sherwood number). If the rate rises, k_ga was limiting (Case II, C_{As}\to0). If nothing happens, you are kinetically controlled (Case I, C_{As}\approx C_{Ab}) — then raise T instead, since only k_s is strongly temperature-sensitive.
24Initial-rate data: how do you name the rate-limiting step? notes
Plot -r_{C0} against p_{C0} with no product in the feed. Linear through the origin ⇒ adsorption limiting; rises and saturates ⇒ surface reaction limiting; flat ⇒ desorption limiting.
25State the PSSH in one sentence. notes
The adsorbed intermediates are present in negligible, effectively constant amounts, so their net rates of formation are ~0 — which lets you set r_i/k_i\to0 for every step that is not rate-limiting.
26Why does catalyst shape matter? notes
It fixes the trade-off between surface area/diffusion length and pressure drop (Ergun). Small particles: more area, shorter diffusion path, less voidage, higher \Delta P, bigger pump. Monoliths give low \Delta P and short diffusion lengths but poor radial heat transfer; spheres are cheap but have long diffusion lengths.
27Name the steps of catalyst preparation. notes
Precipitation/gel → decantation/filtration → washing → drying → crushing → calcination (heating without O₂) → impregnation → activation. Supported catalysts impregnate a preformed support, the precursor entering the pores by diffusion plus capillary flow.
28Turnover frequency vs dispersion? notes
TOF = moles converted per mole of active site per second (10⁻⁴–10⁴ s⁻¹) — an activity measure. Dispersion = surface metal atoms ÷ total metal atoms — a utilisation measure. Both require chemisorption to count sites.
